meta.tagline: Spot the reasoning error in a research claim, or call it sound.

cause.name: Cause
cause.text: Errors in reading cause and effect from data.

sample.name: Sample
sample.text: Errors about who or what was studied, and how far the result reaches.

numbers.name: Numbers
numbers.text: Errors in reading statistics, risks and charts.

practice.name: Practice
practice.text: Errors in how the research was analysed, measured and reported.

C01.title: Chocolate for genius
C01.text: Countries that eat more chocolate per person win more Nobel prizes per person. Chocolate boosts brain power, so eat more of it.
C01.why: A country-level correlation is stretched into a causal claim about individual brains. Wealth could drive both, and the data say nothing about whether the laureates ate chocolate.

traps.shared-trend: These are countries compared at one time, not two series drifting over the years.
traps.small-sample: The problem isn't the number of countries; even with 200 the link would not show cause.

C02.title: Breakfast and grades
C02.text: Pupils who eat breakfast every day get better grades than pupils who skip it. Schools should serve breakfast to raise grades.
C02.why: Family routine, income and parental time plausibly drive both breakfast and grades. A trial of school breakfasts would test the policy itself.

traps.reverse-causation: Good grades are unlikely to make children eat breakfast; the stronger worry is a common cause.
traps.ecological: The data are about individual pupils, not school averages.

C03.title: Lazy and low
C03.text: In a one-off survey of 5,000 adults, the least active people were the most depressed. Inactivity causes depression.
C03.why: Depression saps energy and motivation, so low activity may be a symptom rather than a cause. A snapshot can't tell which came first.

traps.ecological: Each point is a person; the link is measured at the individual level.
traps.small-sample: 5,000 people is plenty to estimate the association; the issue is its direction.

C04.title: Phones and myopia
C04.text: From 2000 to 2020, smartphone ownership and short-sightedness in teenagers both rose year after year (r = 0.96). Phones are ruining children's eyes.
C04.why: Two series that both trend upward correlate almost perfectly whatever links them. Myopia was rising before smartphones; compare changes, or individuals, instead.

traps.regression-mean: Nothing was chosen for being extreme; both series climb steadily.
traps.small-sample: The flaw is not the number of years but that any two rising series correlate.

C05.title: Smokers spared
C05.text: Among patients admitted to hospital with a respiratory virus, smokers were less likely than non-smokers to need intensive care. Smoking may protect against severe disease.
C05.why: Hospital admission is caused both by smoking-related illness and by severe infection. Among the admitted, smokers are more often there for other reasons, so they look milder.

traps.reverse-causation: Needing intensive care can't make someone a smoker before admission.
traps.relative-risk: The percentages are given; the problem is who got into the sample.

C06.title: Height doesn't matter
C06.text: Among professional basketball players, taller players score no more points than shorter ones. Height doesn't matter in basketball.
C06.why: Players reach the league by being tall or by being exceptionally skilled. Selecting on that shared outcome hides height's effect among the selected.

traps.not-significant: The study may be precise; the issue is that everyone was selected for being good.
traps.ecological: The data are on individual players.

C07.title: Transplant triumph
C07.text: Counting from the day they joined the waiting list, patients who got a heart transplant lived far longer than those who never did. Transplants work.
C07.why: To get a transplant you had to survive the wait, and that waiting time was credited to the transplant group. Time must be split at the day of surgery.

traps.regression-mean: Patients weren't picked for an extreme value that later fell back.
traps.survivorship: Close, but the precise error is counting waiting time as transplant time.

C08.title: Statins and survival
C08.text: Patients counted as statin users if they filled a prescription within two years of diagnosis; followed from diagnosis, users had 30% lower mortality.
C08.why: Anyone who died before filling a prescription was automatically a non-user. Users were guaranteed to survive until their first fill.

traps.lead-time: Diagnosis date is the same for both groups; the bias comes from how users were defined.
traps.relative-risk: Absolute survival is shown; the error is in the classification of time.

C09.title: App for everyone
C09.text: Our app grew from 1,000 to 64,000 users in six months by doubling every month. At this rate the whole planet will use it within two years.
C09.why: Exponential growth always saturates. A trend observed over six months says nothing about a range millions of times larger.

traps.small-sample: Six data points describe the past well; the error is projecting them far ahead.
traps.regression-mean: Growth wasn't selected for being extreme; it just can't stay exponential.

C10.title: More is better
C10.text: In a trial of doses from 10 to 40 mg, each extra 10 mg cut blood pressure by 4 mmHg. So a 100 mg dose should cut it by 40 mmHg.
C10.why: Dose-response curves usually flatten and side effects rise. Beyond 40 mg there are no data at all.

traps.surrogate: Blood pressure is an accepted outcome here; the problem is the dose range.

C11.title: Green tea cure
C11.text: A compound from green tea shrank tumours in mice by 60%. Drinking green tea fights cancer.
C11.why: Mice, purified compounds and high doses are far from people drinking tea. Most such leads fail in human trials.

traps.trivial-effect: A 60% shrinkage in mice is not small; the leap is from mice to people.
traps.correlation-causation: The mouse study was an experiment, so cause in mice is plausible.

C12.title: Laptops lift scores
C12.text: Schools with more laptops per pupil have higher average test scores. So pupils who use laptops score higher.
C12.why: A school-level link says nothing about which pupils use laptops or how they score. Richer schools may simply have both.

traps.simpsons: No subgroups are reported; the problem is jumping from schools to pupils.
traps.small-sample: The issue is the level of the data, not how many schools there are.

C13.title: Drop out to win
C13.text: We studied 30 of the most successful start-ups; most were founded by people who dropped out of university. Dropping out breeds success.
C13.why: Only winners were studied. Countless dropouts whose start-ups failed are invisible, so the data can't show what predicts success.

traps.small-sample: Even 3,000 winners would mislead; the failures are missing, not the numbers.
traps.regression-mean: No one was picked for an extreme value that later fell back.

C14.title: Funds beat the market
C14.text: The funds in today's database returned 9% a year on average over 15 years, beating the market's 7%. Active funds are worth their fees.
C14.why: Funds that did badly closed or merged and dropped out of today's database, so the average describes survivors only.

traps.regression-mean: Funds weren't chosen for a single extreme year; the closed ones are missing.
traps.trivial-effect: Two points a year compounds to a lot; the problem is which funds are counted.

C15.title: Readers back it
C15.text: An online poll of 50,000 of our readers found 72% think a four-day working week works. The public backs it.
C15.why: Readers of one outlet who choose to vote online are not the public. A large self-selected sample is still biased.

traps.small-sample: 50,000 is a huge sample; size doesn't fix who chose to answer.
traps.trivial-effect: 72% is not a small difference; the problem is who answered.

C16.title: Wired for fairness
C16.text: In a lab game, 120 psychology undergraduates in Ohio gave up money to keep splits fair. Humans are wired for fairness.
C16.why: Students from one university in one country support a claim about them, not about all humans. Fairness norms in such games vary widely across societies.

traps.model-to-human: The participants are people; the gap is between one group of people and all humans.
traps.small-sample: 120 can show the effect in that group; the leap is to 'humans'.

C17.title: Choose hospital A
C17.text: Hospital A: 90% of surgical patients survive. Hospital B: 85%. Hospital B takes most of the region's high-risk cases. Choose A.
C17.why: When one hospital treats the riskiest patients, its overall rate can be lower even if it does better within every risk group. Compare within risk groups.

traps.base-rate: No test or rare condition is being interpreted here.
traps.chart-distortion: The axis starts at 80, but the bigger problem is comparing different case mixes.

C18.title: Kidney stone choice
C18.text: Treatment X had a higher success rate than Y for small stones and for large stones. Overall, Y had the higher success rate, so Y is the better treatment.
C18.why: X was used mostly on harder, large stones. Within each stone size X wins; the pooled rate mixes difficulty with treatment.

traps.subgroup: The split by stone size is the right analysis here, not a fishing trip.
traps.multiple-tests: Only two strata are compared, and both point the same way.

C19.title: Coaching works
C19.text: The 20 schools with the worst test scores were given a coaching scheme. Next year their scores rose by 8 points. The scheme works.
C19.why: Schools picked for an unusually bad year tend to do better next year anyway. Without comparable untreated schools, the rise can't be credited to coaching.

traps.survivorship: All 20 schools are followed; none drop out.
traps.correlation-causation: Defensible in spirit, but the specific trap is choosing schools for an extreme low.

C20.title: Speed cameras
C20.text: Speed cameras were installed at the 50 sites with the most crashes last year. Crashes at those sites fell by 40% the year after.
C20.why: Sites chosen for a peak year would have fewer crashes next year even without cameras. Part of the 40% is regression to the mean.

traps.relative-risk: The counts per site are shown; the problem is how the sites were picked.
traps.unrepresentative: The cameras are meant for high-crash sites; the issue is the comparison over time.

C21.title: Cancer village
C21.text: The town with the highest rate of a rare cancer in the country has only 900 inhabitants. Something in that town must be causing it.
C21.why: Two cases in 900 people give a rate of 220 per 100,000. Among thousands of small towns, some will top the table by chance.

traps.ecological: The claim is about the town itself, not about individuals inside it.
traps.relative-risk: Absolute rates are given; the issue is how unstable they are in a tiny town.

C22.title: Small schools rule
C22.text: Most of the top 50 schools in the national ranking are small schools. Splitting big schools into small ones will raise results.
C22.why: Small schools' averages swing more, so they crowd both the top and the bottom of any ranking. Look at the bottom 50 too.

traps.survivorship: No schools are missing from the ranking.
traps.weird: The issue isn't the kind of school sampled but how much small schools vary.

C23.title: Spot the terrorist
C23.text: A new face-scanning system spots known suspects with 99% accuracy. So anyone it flags at the airport is almost certainly a suspect.
C23.why: Among millions of travellers and a handful of suspects, 1% false alarms means thousands of innocent people flagged for every real suspect.

traps.trivial-effect: The accuracy is high; the trouble is how rare suspects are.
traps.overfitting: Perhaps, but even a perfectly validated 99% would mislead here.

C24.title: Positive test
C24.text: A test finds 95% of cancers and wrongly flags 5% of healthy people. One in 200 people screened has the cancer. You tested positive, so it's about 95% likely you have it.
C24.why: Per 10,000 screened: 48 true positives and about 500 false ones. A positive result means roughly a 9% chance of cancer.

traps.lead-time: No survival figure is being interpreted.

C25.title: One per cent chance
C25.text: Our experiment gave p = 0.01, so there is only a 1% chance that the effect isn't real.
C25.why: p is the probability of data this extreme if there were no effect, not the probability that there is no effect. That depends on prior plausibility too.

traps.trivial-effect: We don't know the effect size; the error is in reading the p-value.
traps.not-significant: The result is significant; the misreading runs the other way.

C26.title: DNA match
C26.text: The suspect's DNA matches the crime scene. Only 1 in a million people would match by chance, so the chance he is innocent is 1 in a million.
C26.why: In a city of 5 million, about five people would match by chance. P(match | innocent) is not P(innocent | match).

traps.small-sample: The match probability isn't unstable; it's being turned inside out.
traps.multiple-tests: Defensible only if a database was trawled; the core error is the transposed conditional.

C27.title: Painkiller flops
C27.text: In a trial of 60 patients, the new painkiller cut pain by 1.5 points on a 10-point scale (95% CI −0.2 to 3.2; not significant). The drug doesn't work.
C27.why: The interval runs from no effect to a large one. A small trial that can't rule out a big benefit hasn't shown that the drug fails.

traps.trivial-effect: The estimate isn't trivially small; it is uncertain.
traps.p-hacking: There's no sign of flexible analysis; the problem is the conclusion.

C28.title: Clicks for the win
C28.text: Across 2 million users, the new button colour raised clicks from 3.00% to 3.02% (p < 0.001). A major success for the design team.
C28.why: With millions of users, a difference of 0.02 percentage points is 'significant' but hardly matters. Ask how big, in units that count.

traps.small-sample: Two million users is the opposite problem.
traps.not-significant: The result is significant; that's not the issue.

C29.title: Screens and sadness
C29.text: In 300,000 teenagers, more screen time went with lower wellbeing (p < 0.0001). Screens are harming a generation.
C29.why: A tiny p-value in a huge sample can come from a correlation near zero. How much wellbeing varies with screen time matters more, and the design can't show cause.

traps.small-sample: 300,000 is a very large sample.
traps.ecological: The data are on individual teenagers.

C30.title: Night-shift tumour
C30.text: Headline: night-shift work raises the risk of a rare tumour by 50%!
C30.why: 50% more of a rare tumour may mean 3 cases per 100,000 instead of 2. Without the absolute numbers the headline can't be judged.

traps.trivial-effect: Close, but you can't judge size until you know the starting risk.
traps.base-rate: No test result is being interpreted; ask for the absolute risk.

C31.title: Screening halves deaths
C31.text: Our screening programme halves your risk of dying from cancer X! (Ten-year trial.)
C31.why: Halving 2 in 1,000 to 1 in 1,000 saves one person per 1,000 screened over ten years. The relative figure alone oversells it.

traps.lead-time: The trial counts deaths, not survival after diagnosis, so lead time doesn't apply.
traps.chart-distortion: The axis starts at zero and the bars are honest; the slogan isn't.

C32.title: Support surges
C32.text: Support for the policy has surged since our campaign began.
C32.why: The axis starts at 48%, so a three-point change looks like a fourfold rise. Within normal polling error, support barely moved.

traps.regression-mean: Nothing was selected for an extreme value.
traps.correlation-causation: Defensible, but first notice how small the change is.

C33.title: Jobs turnaround
C33.text: Since March, unemployment has fallen every month. The new jobs policy is working.
C33.why: Five months on a cropped axis hide what came before: was March a spike? Plot the longer series and compare with places without the policy.

traps.small-sample: The numbers come from a large labour survey; the window is the problem.
traps.changed-yardstick: No change in definition is mentioned.

C34.title: Election oracle
C34.text: Our model uses 200 variables and correctly called 149 of last year's 150 districts. It will predict the next election just as well.
C34.why: With more variables than cases, a model can memorise the past. Only predictions for elections it hasn't seen show its real accuracy.

traps.base-rate: No rare condition is being tested for.
traps.small-sample: Close, but the giveaway is 200 variables fitted to 150 cases.

C35.title: Winning rule
C35.text: We tested 10,000 trading rules on 20 years of prices. The best one beat the market every single year in the back-test. Invest with it.
C35.why: The best of 10,000 rules fitted to the same history will look brilliant by chance. Test it on later data it was never tuned on.

traps.survivorship: Related, but the best of 10,000 tries is the core problem.
traps.regression-mean: Expect future returns to fall back, but name the cause: the rule was fitted to noise.

C36.title: Warm cup, warm heart
C36.text: After excluding outliers and adjusting for age and mood, participants who held a warm cup rated a stranger as friendlier (p = 0.048).
C36.why: Outlier rules and covariates chosen after seeing the data, and a p-value just under 0.05, suggest a forking path. Was this analysis preregistered?

traps.not-significant: The result is (just) significant; the worry is how it got there.
traps.trivial-effect: We don't know the effect size; the analysis choices are the red flag.

C37.title: Tomatoes and migraine
C37.text: We tested 40 foods against 12 diseases. Eating tomatoes was linked to fewer migraines (p = 0.03).
C37.why: 480 tests at p < 0.05 would give about 24 'hits' if nothing were real. One of them is not news.

traps.small-sample: The sample size isn't given; 480 tests is the problem.
traps.trivial-effect: We don't know the size; the hit itself may be noise.

C38.title: Women over 65
C38.text: Overall, the drug did not prevent strokes. But in women over 65 it cut strokes by 40% (p = 0.02). It should be approved for them.
C38.why: Was this subgroup planned, and does it pass an interaction test? A lone subgroup effect in a null trial is usually chance.

traps.simpsons: The overall and subgroup results don't reverse; one slice stands out.
traps.weird: The subgroup is chosen after the fact; that's the issue, not the sample's breadth.

C39.title: Brain games
C39.text: A meta-analysis of 25 published studies concludes that brain-training games raise IQ by 5 points.
C39.why: If studies that found nothing stayed in the file drawer, pooling the published ones overstates the effect. Check registries and funnel plots.

traps.single-study: It pools 25 studies; the question is which studies got published.
traps.small-sample: Small studies may be the symptom; the missing ones are the cause.

C40.title: Stand to remember
C40.text: A new study of 40 students found that standing while studying improves memory by 20%. Schools should buy standing desks.
C40.why: One small, new study is a lead, not a basis for policy. Wait for replications.

traps.publication-bias: Only one study is cited; there's nothing yet to be biased.

C41.title: Good cholesterol
C41.text: Our drug raised 'good' HDL cholesterol by 70% in a large trial. It will prevent heart attacks.
C41.why: Raising a marker isn't the same as preventing the outcome. A drug in this class raised HDL and increased deaths and cardiovascular events.

traps.relative-risk: The 70% is a change in a blood value, not a risk.
traps.correlation-causation: The drug did cause the HDL rise; the leap is from marker to outcome.

C42.title: Survival soars
C42.text: Since screening began, five-year survival for prostate cancer rose from 70% to 98%. Screening is saving lives.
C42.why: Screening diagnoses earlier and finds slow tumours, so survival from diagnosis rises even if no one lives longer. Mortality is the test.

traps.relative-risk: No relative risk is quoted; the measure itself misleads.
traps.regression-mean: No group was selected for an extreme value.

C43.title: ADHD epidemic
C43.text: Recorded diagnoses of ADHD doubled in ten years, a period that included a new edition of the diagnostic manual. We face an epidemic.
C43.why: New criteria, awareness and services change how many cases are recorded. A rise in diagnoses is not the same as a rise in the condition.

traps.small-sample: Recorded diagnoses cover the whole population.
traps.regression-mean: The rise is steady, not a bounce from an extreme year.

C44.title: Hate crime quadruples
C44.text: Police-recorded hate crime has quadrupled in a decade in which forces were told to improve how they record it. Prejudice is surging.
C44.why: Better recording, and more people reporting, raise the count without more crime. Victim surveys measure it the same way each year.

traps.small-sample: These are national counts.

C45.title: More police, more crime
C45.text: Cities with more police officers per resident have more crime. Police presence causes crime.
C45.why: Cities hire more police because they have more crime. The arrow most plausibly runs from crime to police.

traps.ecological: Defensible to note, but the claim is about cities, and the arrow is the real issue.

C46.title: Vaccine trial
C46.text: In a preregistered trial, 8,000 adults were randomly given the vaccine or a placebo. Confirmed infections: 0.4% vs 2.0% (difference 1.6 points, 95% CI 1.2 to 2.0).
C46.why: Random allocation, a registered plan, absolute risks and a confidence interval: the claim says no more than the trial shows.

traps.correlation-causation: Randomisation balances known and unknown factors, so cause is warranted.
traps.small-sample: 8,000 people give a tight interval.

C47.title: Twelve trials
C47.text: A review of all 12 registered trials, including three whose results were obtained from trial registries, found the drug lowered stroke deaths, with consistent results.
C47.why: Searching registries closes the file drawer, and consistency across 12 trials makes chance unlikely.

traps.publication-bias: Unpublished results were retrieved from registries.

C48.title: Screening trial
C48.text: In a randomised trial of 50,000 people followed for 15 years, 0.9% of the screened group and 1.2% of the unscreened group died of bowel cancer.
C48.why: Comparing mortality between randomised groups is immune to lead time and overdiagnosis, and the absolute difference is stated.

traps.lead-time: The outcome is deaths among everyone randomised, not survival after diagnosis.

C49.title: Positive, then what?
C49.text: Of 10,000 people tested, about 100 have the disease. The test flags 95 of them and 495 of the healthy. So a positive result means about a 1 in 6 chance of disease.
C49.why: Natural frequencies make the reasoning transparent: 95 true positives among 590 positives is about 16%.

traps.base-rate: The base rate is used correctly: 95 of 590 positives are true.
traps.inverse-probability: The probability is computed the right way round.

C50.title: Precise null
C50.text: A trial of 20,000 people found the supplement changed fracture risk by −0.2 points (95% CI −0.6 to +0.2). Any benefit is too small to matter.
C50.why: A narrow interval around zero is evidence of absence of a meaningful effect, and the claim stays within it.

traps.not-significant: The claim rests on a narrow interval that rules out meaningful effects, not on p > 0.05.
traps.small-sample: 20,000 people is large.

C51.title: Both groups fell
C51.text: People with high blood-pressure readings were randomised to a coaching programme or usual care. Both groups' pressure fell, but the programme group's fell 6 mmHg more.
C51.why: A randomised control group experiences the same regression to the mean, so the difference between groups is a fair estimate.

traps.regression-mean: Both groups regress equally; the 6 mmHg extra drop is the effect.
traps.surrogate: Blood pressure is a well-validated outcome for this purpose, and the claim is only about blood pressure.

C52.title: Validated model
C52.text: A readmission model built on 2015–19 data from one hospital was tested on 40,000 patients from five other hospitals in 2021. It ranked patients correctly 78% of the time.
C52.why: External, temporal validation is the right test of a prediction model, and 78% is reported as modest, not perfect.

traps.overfitting: Performance is reported on new hospitals and a later year.
traps.extrapolation: The test data cover the setting the claim is about.

C53.title: Every school
C53.text: In a trial randomising classes within 14 schools, the new method beat the old one in every school and overall.
C53.why: Randomisation within schools and a consistent effect across all of them make the overall claim trustworthy.

traps.simpsons: The effect is the same in every school and overall, so pooling hides nothing.
traps.ecological: Classes were randomised and outcomes measured on pupils.

C54.title: Older Dutch adults
C54.text: In a randomised trial of 2,000 Dutch adults over 70, balance classes cut falls by 20%. The authors recommend them for older adults in similar settings.
C54.why: A randomised trial with a claim that stays within the population studied, and absolute figures on the chart.

traps.weird: The claim is limited to similar older adults, the population studied.
traps.relative-risk: The chart gives the absolute percentages.

C55.title: Smoking ban
C55.text: After a region banned smoking in bars, heart-attack admissions fell 12% compared with neighbouring regions without a ban; the two had moved together for five years before.
C55.why: A comparison group with parallel pre-trends is a strong design for a policy that can't be randomised.

traps.shared-trend: The comparison regions share the same trends; the drop appears only after the ban.
traps.regression-mean: The region wasn't chosen for an extreme year; the pre-period was stable.

C56.title: Safer cycling
C56.text: Between 2010 and 2020, cyclist deaths per billion kilometres cycled in the city fell from 30 to 15. The risk per kilometre has halved.
C56.why: Deaths are expressed per distance cycled, so more cycling is accounted for, and the chart is honest.

traps.relative-risk: The claim is about a rate, and both rates are given.

C57.title: Smoking and cancer
C57.text: Hundreds of studies in dozens of countries link smoking to lung cancer, with risk rising with dose and smoking recorded years before diagnosis.
C57.why: Strength, consistency, dose-response and temporality: the classic case where observational evidence supports cause.

traps.correlation-causation: Consistency, dose-response and timing together make a causal reading justified.
traps.reverse-causation: Smoking was recorded years before diagnosis.

C58.title: Planned subgroup
C58.text: The drug helped patients with poor kidney function more, a subgroup named in the registered protocol, with a significant interaction test, confirmed in a second trial.
C58.why: Subgroup claims are credible when planned, few, tested as interactions and replicated. This one is.

traps.subgroup: Prespecified, tested as an interaction and replicated: this subgroup effect meets the credibility criteria.
traps.multiple-tests: One planned subgroup, not a trawl.

C59.title: Real progress
C59.text: In a randomised trial of 3,000 pupils, the reading programme raised reading scores by 0.4 standard deviations, roughly four months of extra progress.
C59.why: A randomised design, a large sample and an effect size translated into months of progress.

traps.trivial-effect: The size is given in meaningful units, and it is substantial.
traps.surrogate: Reading scores are the outcome the programme aims at.

C60.title: All the funds
C60.text: Including all 412 funds launched since 2005, the 180 that closed among them, active funds returned 1.2% a year less than the index.
C60.why: Counting the funds that closed removes survivorship bias, and the claim only describes what happened.

traps.small-sample: 412 funds over many years is a solid base for an average.

correlation-causation.name: Correlation as causation
correlation-causation.short: Two things go together, so one is said to cause the other.
correlation-causation.text: An association alone cannot tell cause from chance, a shared cause or reverse causation. A causal claim needs a design or analysis that rules those out.
correlation-causation.example: Matthews (2000): across 17 European countries, stork pairs correlated with birth rates (r ≈ 0.62, p = 0.008).

confounding.name: Hidden third factor
confounding.short: Something else drives both the supposed cause and the outcome.
confounding.text: A confounder causes both the exposure and the outcome, so the two move together even if one has no effect on the other.
confounding.example: HRT looked heart-protective in observational studies; the WHI trial (2002) found a higher coronary risk (HR 1.29).

reverse-causation.name: Reverse causation
reverse-causation.short: The outcome may be causing the supposed cause.
reverse-causation.text: When exposure and outcome are measured together, the arrow can point the other way: illness changes habits, poor results change policies.
reverse-causation.example: Shaper et al. (1988): non-drinkers' higher death rates partly reflected ill men who had stopped drinking.

shared-trend.name: Two trends, one clock
shared-trend.short: Two series that both drift over time correlate, whatever links them.
shared-trend.text: Anything that rises or falls steadily over the years correlates with anything else that does. Compare year-on-year changes, not levels.
shared-trend.example: Yule (1926): Church of England marriages and mortality in England and Wales, 1866–1911, correlated at r = 0.95.

collider.name: Collider bias
collider.short: Selecting on a shared consequence creates a link that isn't there.
collider.text: If only cases with a common effect are studied (hospital patients, published papers, low-weight babies), two unrelated causes of it appear linked.
collider.example: Birth-weight paradox: among low-birth-weight babies, maternal smoking looked protective (Hernández-Díaz et al. 2006).

immortal-time.name: Immortal time
immortal-time.short: A group is defined by something later, so its members had to survive to join it.
immortal-time.text: Counting the time before someone becomes 'exposed' as exposed time gives that group a head start in survival it did not earn.
immortal-time.example: Oscar winners seemed to live 3.9 years longer; counted correctly, the gap shrank to about 1 year (Sylvestre et al. 2006).

extrapolation.name: Beyond the data
extrapolation.short: A trend is stretched far past the range where it was observed.
extrapolation.text: A pattern seen over one range of doses, ages or years need not hold outside it. Straight lines rarely stay straight.
extrapolation.example: Tatem et al. (2004) extended Olympic 100 m trends to predict that women would outrun men in 2156.

model-to-human.name: Mice to people
model-to-human.short: A result in cells, animals or simulations is claimed for people.
model-to-human.text: Models are where hypotheses start. Many effects found in cells or animals shrink, vanish or reverse in human trials.
model-to-human.example: TGN1412 (2006): a dose 1/500 of the level safe in monkeys gave all six volunteers a severe inflammatory reaction.

ecological.name: Ecological fallacy
ecological.short: A pattern across groups is read as true of the individuals in them.
ecological.text: Countries, regions or schools can show a correlation that runs the other way, or not at all, among the people inside them.
ecological.example: US 1930: states with more immigrants had less illiteracy (r ≈ −0.53), yet immigrants were slightly more often illiterate.

survivorship.name: Survivorship bias
survivorship.short: Only the cases that made it through are looked at.
survivorship.text: Failed firms, closed funds, dropped-out patients and lost planes leave no data. Studying the survivors shows what survival looks like, not what causes it.
survivorship.example: WWII: Wald used damage on returning bombers to estimate vulnerability; places rarely hit on survivors were likely the deadliest.

unrepresentative.name: Unrepresentative sample
unrepresentative.short: The people who answered differ from the people the claim is about.
unrepresentative.text: A huge sample does not fix a skewed one. Volunteers, online panels and readers of one magazine are not the population.
unrepresentative.example: Literary Digest, 1936: about 2.4 million returned ballots predicted Landon; Roosevelt won in a landslide.

weird.name: Narrow sample, universal claim
weird.short: One kind of participant, a claim about all humans.
weird.text: Results from students, one country or one culture are written up as facts about people in general.
weird.example: Henrich et al. (2010): 96% of psychology samples came from countries with 12% of the world's population.

simpsons.name: Simpson's paradox
simpsons.short: A trend in the pooled data reverses or vanishes within every subgroup.
simpsons.text: When groups differ in size and baseline, adding them together can flip a comparison. The right level depends on the causal question.
simpsons.example: Berkeley, 1973: 44% of men vs 35% of women admitted, but department by department there was little bias.

regression-mean.name: Regression to the mean
regression-mean.short: Extreme values drift back toward average on their own.
regression-mean.text: Anything picked because it was unusually high or low tends to be less extreme next time, with or without the treatment.
regression-mean.example: Galton (1886): children of very tall or very short parents were, on average, closer to the mean height.

small-sample.name: Small numbers, wild swings
small-sample.short: Small groups give extreme results by chance, at both ends.
small-sample.text: The fewer the cases, the more a rate jumps around. The best and the worst of a league table are often just the smallest.
small-sample.example: Wainer (2007): US counties with the lowest kidney-cancer rates were mostly small and rural, and so were the highest.

base-rate.name: Base-rate neglect
base-rate.short: How rare the condition is gets ignored.
base-rate.text: When something is rare, even an accurate test or detector produces mostly false alarms. The base rate decides what a positive result means.
base-rate.example: Casscells et al. (1978): most Harvard clinicians put a positive test at 95% likely true; at 1-in-1,000 prevalence it is about 2%.

inverse-probability.name: Transposed conditional
inverse-probability.short: The chance of the data given a hypothesis is read as the chance of the hypothesis.
inverse-probability.text: P(evidence | innocent) is not P(innocent | evidence), and p = 0.01 is not a 1% chance that the effect is a fluke.
inverse-probability.example: Sally Clark trial: press reported '1 in 73 million' as the chance the two deaths were accidental (RSS, 2002).

not-significant.name: No significance, no effect
not-significant.short: A non-significant result is reported as proof of no effect.
not-significant.text: Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence. A wide confidence interval that includes zero also includes effects worth caring about.
not-significant.example: Amrhein et al. (2019): a risk ratio of 1.2 with P = 0.091 was reported as 'no association'.

trivial-effect.name: Significant but trivial
trivial-effect.short: A tiny effect is sold as important because p is small.
trivial-effect.text: With a big enough sample, almost any difference is 'significant'. Statistical significance says nothing about size or importance.
trivial-effect.example: Kramer et al. (2014): with 689,003 Facebook users, effects as small as d = 0.001 were statistically significant.

relative-risk.name: Relative risk alone
relative-risk.short: 'Doubles the risk' without saying risk of what, from how much.
relative-risk.text: A 100% rise from 1 in 7,000 is 1 extra case in 7,000. Without the absolute numbers, a relative change can't be judged.
relative-risk.example: UK 1995: a warning that newer pills doubled clot risk (about 1 to 2 in 7,000) was followed by some 13,000 extra abortions.

chart-distortion.name: Distorted chart
chart-distortion.short: The picture exaggerates what the numbers say.
chart-distortion.text: A cut-off axis, two different scales or a stretched time window can make a small change look dramatic, or a big one vanish.
chart-distortion.example: A 2015 US House hearing chart used two unlabelled scales, so ~327,000 abortions seemed to overtake ~935,000 cancer screenings.

overfitting.name: Overfitting
overfitting.short: A model fits the past perfectly and predicts the future badly.
overfitting.text: Many predictors and few cases let a model learn the noise. Only performance on new data shows what it really knows.
overfitting.example: Google Flu Trends overestimated flu in 100 of 108 weeks from August 2011, more than double in February 2013 (Lazer et al. 2014).

p-hacking.name: Forking paths
p-hacking.short: The analysis was chosen after seeing the data.
p-hacking.text: Trying other outcomes, covariates, exclusions or stopping points until p < 0.05 makes false positives likely, even without bad intent.
p-hacking.example: Simmons et al. (2011): flexible analysis 'showed' that hearing a Beatles song made people nearly 18 months younger.

multiple-tests.name: Many tests, one hit
multiple-tests.short: Out of many comparisons, the one that came up significant is reported.
multiple-tests.text: Test 20 true nulls at p < 0.05 and expect one hit. Without correction, a lone significant result among many is likely noise.
multiple-tests.example: Bennett et al. (2009): uncorrected fMRI tests found 'active' voxels in a dead salmon shown photos of people.

subgroup.name: Subgroup surprise
subgroup.short: The effect is claimed for one subgroup found after the fact.
subgroup.text: Slice a trial enough ways and some slice will differ by chance. Credible subgroup effects are few, prespecified and tested as interactions.
subgroup.example: ISIS-2 (1988): aspirin helped after heart attack, except, apparently, in patients born under Gemini or Libra.

publication-bias.name: File drawer
publication-bias.short: The published studies are the ones that worked.
publication-bias.text: Null results stay unpublished, so the literature, and any review of it, overstates the effect.
publication-bias.example: Turner et al. (2008): 94% of published antidepressant trials looked positive; by FDA review, 51% were.

single-study.name: One study, settled
single-study.short: One striking study is treated as established fact.
single-study.text: A first result, especially a small and surprising one, is a lead to follow up. Many fail to replicate.
single-study.example: Power posing (2010, 42 people) reported hormone changes; a 200-person replication found none (Ranehill et al. 2015).

surrogate.name: Surrogate endpoint
surrogate.short: A marker improved, so people are assumed to be better off.
surrogate.text: Blood values, test scores and clicks stand in for what matters. Changing the marker need not change the outcome, and can worsen it.
surrogate.example: CAST (1991): drugs suppressed irregular heartbeats, yet 63 patients died on drug vs 26 on placebo.

lead-time.name: Survival-time illusion
lead-time.short: Earlier diagnosis lengthens survival without delaying death.
lead-time.text: Screening starts the clock sooner and finds harmless cases, so survival after diagnosis rises even if no one lives longer. Look at mortality.
lead-time.example: South Korea: screening raised thyroid-cancer diagnoses 15-fold by 2011 while deaths stayed flat (Ahn et al. 2014).

changed-yardstick.name: Changed yardstick
changed-yardstick.short: The count rose because the definition or the counting changed.
changed-yardstick.text: New criteria, more testing or better reporting can create a rise or fall in the numbers with no change in the world.
changed-yardstick.example: Denmark: about 60% of the rise in autism diagnoses was explained by changed criteria and reporting (Hansen et al. 2015).

denominator.name: Ask for the denominator
denominator.short: Out of how many? Turn counts and percentages back into natural frequencies.
denominator.text: Ask how common the thing is to begin with, and what the numbers are out of. Base rates, absolute risks and the reverse probability fall out of one 2×2 table.

comparison.name: Compared with what?
comparison.short: Ask for the group that didn't get it, over the same time.
comparison.text: A change or a link means little without a fair comparison: a control group, the same people before, or similar places that were left alone.

causal-diagram.name: Draw the causal diagram
causal-diagram.short: Sketch what causes what, then look for back doors and colliders.
causal-diagram.text: Draw arrows between exposure, outcome and everything that affects them. Paths through a common cause need adjusting for; a common effect must not be selected on.

timeline.name: Check the timeline
timeline.short: What came first, and when did each person's clock start?
timeline.text: Line up when exposure, diagnosis, follow-up and outcome happened. Causes come first; follow-up starts at the same moment for every group.

over-time.name: Plot it over time
over-time.short: Look at the whole series, not two points or one stretch.
over-time.text: A longer series shows trends, bounces back to normal and breaks where a definition changed. Compare year-on-year changes, not levels.

split.name: Split by subgroup
split.short: Break the total down by the variable that differs between groups.
split.text: Look within departments, hospitals, age bands or severity levels. If the comparison flips, decide which level answers the question.

individuals.name: Ask for individual data
individuals.short: Do the same people have both traits, or only the same places?
individuals.text: A claim about people needs data on people. Group averages can't show who within the group has the exposure and the outcome.

missing.name: Find who's missing
missing.short: Who dropped out, failed, didn't answer or never got in?
missing.text: List how cases reached the data set. Survivors, responders, admitted patients and published studies are filtered, and the filter can create the result.

range.name: Check who and what was studied
range.short: Which people, species, doses and years does the evidence cover?
range.text: Compare the claim's reach with the data's range. Outside the studied population, dose or period, the result is a hypothesis.

prereg.name: Find the preregistration
prereg.short: Was this outcome and analysis planned before the data came in?
prereg.text: Look for a trial registration or preregistered plan and compare it with the paper. Switched outcomes and unplanned subgroups are exploratory.

replicate.name: Look for the other studies
replicate.short: Has it been replicated? What do registries and reviews show?
replicate.text: Search for replications, systematic reviews and registered trials, including unpublished ones. One result is a lead; a body of evidence is a finding.

interval.name: Read the confidence interval
interval.short: Look at the range of effects the data allow, not just the p-value.
interval.text: A wide interval means the data are compatible with large effects in both directions, or none. Small samples give wide intervals.

effect-size.name: Ask how big
effect-size.short: How large is the effect in units that matter to people?
effect-size.text: Ask for the absolute difference, the number needed to treat, or the effect in real units, and compare it with what would matter in practice.

outcome.name: Ask what was measured
outcome.short: Is the outcome the thing we care about, measured the same way throughout?
outcome.text: Check whether the result is a marker or the real endpoint, and whether definitions, tests or screening changed during the study.

new-data.name: Test it on new data
new-data.short: How well does it predict cases it has never seen?
new-data.text: Ask for performance on held-out or later data, or an external validation. Fit on the data used to build a model is always flattering.

axis.name: Read the axes
axis.short: Where does each axis start, and are the scales the same?
axis.text: Check the axis start, units, scale and time window. Redraw from zero, or on one scale, and see if the story survives.
